title: Why cats' eyes glow in the dark
pause_note: v5, first Animals Explained Short. WEIRD hook: glowing cat eyes in a flashlight beam at 0 s, a human face that does not glow at ~2.5 s; wrong guess (the eyes make light) killed at ~4.5 s; reveal (mirror layer behind the retina) at ~8 s; second pass, leak = the glow; stake (a sixth of the light, a bit blurrier); one-word question; loop.

beats: Shine a light at a cat in the dark, and its eyes light up. Yours don't.
Cat eyes don't make light. They bounce yours back.
Behind the retina sits a mirror layer, the tapetum lucidum.
Light that slips past the retina hits it, and goes back through for a second chance.
Some of it escapes, straight back toward your light. That's the glow.
So a cat sees with about a sixth of the light you need. The price: a slightly blurrier picture.
Your cat's eyes: green or gold?
